metadata.title: Where the Light Goes: light, pressure and bioluminescence in the ocean

canonical_sources.title: How far does light travel in the ocean?
Why is the ocean blue? / red light is filtered out first
Quantification of bioluminescence from the surface to the deep sea demonstrates its predominance as an ecological trait
canonical_sources.authors: Séverine Martini, Steven H. D. Haddock

pedagogy.problem_statement: The sea looks bright at the surface and black below. Where does the light go, and is the dark really empty?
pedagogy.core_thesis: Sunlight is absorbed within a thousand metres, colour by colour, but most deep-sea animals produce their own light.
pedagogy.mental_model: A descent in which the world loses colour, gains weight, and then lights itself.
pedagogy.key_takeaway: Below the sunlight, the deep sea is dark of sunlight but full of animal-made light.
verified_claims: Light may be detected as far as 1,000 m down, but there is rarely any significant light beyond 200 m [NOAA Ocean Service].
The upper 200 m is the euphotic (sunlight) zone; 200-1,000 m is the twilight (dysphotic) zone; below 1,000 m sunlight does not penetrate (aphotic) [NOAA Ocean Service].
Blue light penetrates best; red light is quickly filtered out as depth increases [NOAA Ocean Exploration].
Water pressure increases by about one atmosphere for every 10 m (33 ft) of depth [NOAA PMEL].
The Challenger Deep is roughly 10,900-11,000 m deep, so the rule gives roughly 1,100 atmospheres there [NOAA depth sources; the figure is the rule applied, not a measurement].
In 17 years of ROV video off California, from the surface to 3,900 m, 76% of observed individuals were bioluminescent (over 350,000 observations) [Martini & Haddock 2017, via the Europe PMC record].
anti_patterns: Do not state the 76% as a global figure
Do not give an exact depth at which red disappears (the consulted NOAA pages give none)
Do not describe procedural imagery as footage
Do not call the deep sea empty

equations.spoken_form: pressure rises about one atmosphere for every ten metres
equations.context: Rule of thumb for seawater (NOAA PMEL)

algorithmic_steps.state_effect: red filtered first; blue goes deepest
